parties.label: RESPONDEN
names: KL PETROGAS SDN BHD (DI BAWAH PENERIMAAN)

judgments.catchwords: whether a debt financing agreement in the form of a “whole turnover agreement”, had breached s 5(1) of the Moneylenders Act 1951 (MA). A whole turnover agreement between a financier (X) and borrower (Y) provides for - (1) X to advance money to Y with Y’s assignment to X of all of Y’s “future receivables” or Y’s future book debts (Y’s Assignment); and (2) Y’s Assignment shall take effect on a date stated in the whole turnover agreement which is - (a) before Y has issued any invoice to Y’s debtor(s); (b) before Y’s receivables are due to be paid to Y; and (c) before any debt has accrued in favour of Y and is payable to Y. A whole turnover agreement is also known as a “receivables purchase agreement”, “whole turnover factoring” and “whole turnover invoice discounting”.

judgments.catchwords: Keywords: Appeal on Enclosure 131 – application by the First Defendant (“D1”) to set aside the Judgment in Default (JID) – filed on 14 May 2026 after the Court of Appeal on 30 April 2026 – set aside a previous High Court order – granted D1 the liberty to file a fresh application – also a Notice of Discontinuation (NOD) – by D1’s Solicitors on D1’s Counterclaim – the Plaintiffs attempted to serve on D1 the cause papers at D1’s resident address – Plaintiffs applied for an Order for Substituted Service (SS) and obtained an order to that effect on 10 October 2012 – cause papers were served on D1 by way of SS Order dated 19 February 2013 to D1’s last known address – D1 failed to enter his appearance and as a result, the Plaintiffs’ Solicitors filed an application on 22 May 2013 to obtain leave of this Court to enter JID against D1 and 3rd Defendant – D1 was made bankrupt – D1 submitted his “Borang Pernyataan Hal Ehwal” dated 6 November 2023 admitting and acknowledging his liability under the JID of 31 May 2013 (Enclosure 139, paragraph 41) – The Director of Insolvency (DGI) approved and confirmed the debt due to the Plaintiffs – D1’s Solicitors then applied to annul the RO & AO – the judgment debt under the JID has been settled in full – D1 filed a Notice of Application for an extension of time to file an application to set aside the JID dated 31 May 2012 - D1 did not disclose the fact that D1 had settled the judgment debt – D1 obtained an Order from the High Court Kuala Lumpur that the JID dated 31 May 2013 was set aside – 1st Plaintiff filed a Notice of Appeal to the Court of Appeal – Court of Appeal directed with a consent judgment that D1 is granted liberty to file an application to set aside the JID – the matter is remitted back to the Kuala Lumpur High court with no order as to cost – 1st Plaintiff’s counsel wrote to D1’s Solicitors with a view that D1’s Counterclaim is left without cause as the previous Kuala Lumpur High Court’s Order was set aside by the COA – Court’s first duty is to determine if the JID was obtained regularly or irregularly – If the judgment is irregular then it ought to be set aside – if it is regularly obtained, as decided by the Federal Court – must show that he has defence on the merits – finding is that the JID was regularly obtained following the SS – SS was not challenged – there was no cross appeal by D1 on the SS – previous Kuala Lumpur High Court thought allowed the setting aside of JID, found that the service of the JID was regularly obtained – inordinate delay of almost thirteen (13) years since the JID was entered – Order 42 Rule 13 of the Rules of Court 2012 (ROC 2012), an application to set aside a judgment must be made within 30 days of receipt. D1 admitted to having knowledge of the JID since late 2013 – yet he failed to take any immediate steps to set it aside – Lack of Merits and Improper Supporting Evidence – Improper Deponent – the affidavit in support – was affirmed by the D1’s solicitor – affidavit – contained facts – not within the solicitor’s personal knowledge – legal principles established that a solicitor should not depose an affidavit on behalf of a litigant if the facts are contentious or involve disputed questions of fact – act of the solicitor deposing a contentious affidavit for D1 was a clear breach of Rule 28 of the Legal Profession (Practice and Etiquette) Rules 1978 – application is substantively defective as D1 failed to produce a draft proposed defensed or demonstrate any arguable or triable issues – failure to disclose material facts by D1 including the fact that an identical challenge to the service of the Writ had already been heard and rejected by the High Court in a previous application – the D1 had voluntarily admitted and settled the judgment debt in full to obtain an annulment of his bankruptcy – that D1 acknowledge and accepted the judgment debt – First Defendant is estopped from challenging the judgment due to his subsequent conduct – estoppe

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v MOHD NOR KHAIRI BIN NOSOHA & ors
judgments.catchwords: (1)(a) when a criminal appeal is lodged by the Public Prosecutor (PP) to the Court of Appeal against a decision of the High Court which concerns more than one accused person (Appeal); (b) one accused person (X) could not be present in the Court of Appeal even though the Court of Appeal has conducted previous mentions and/or case management (CM) for the Appeal; and (c) the co-accused person (Y) is present in the Court of Appeal and the PP has a discretion to proceed with the Appeal against Y only but the PP does not choose to do so - does the Court of Appeal have a discretion to strike out the Appeal pursuant to the second limb of r 105 (to prevent an abuse of process of the Court of Appeal) of the Rules of the Court of Appeal 1994 (RCA)?; and (2) if the Court of Appeal strikes out the Appeal [Court of Appeal’s Decision (Striking Out of Appeal)] - (a) can the PP subsequently apply to the Court of Appeal to reinstate the Appeal under the first limb of r 105 RCA (to prevent injustice) read with r 1A RCA, so as proceed with the Appeal against - (i) Y only; or (ii) X and Y; and (b) in view of the definition of “decision” in s 3 of the Courts of Judicature Act 1964 (CJA) and s 87(1) CJA, can the PP appeal to the Federal Court against the Court of Appeal’s Decision (Striking Out of Appeal)?
coram: YA Datuk Wong Kian Kheong
YA Datuk Hayatul Akmal binti Abdul Aziz
YA Tuan Muniandy a/l Kannyappan

judgments.title: SIVACHANDRAN A/L S JAYARAJAH v Pendakwa Raya
judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.

judgments.catchwords: (1) when the licensed moneylender fails to comply with s 16(1) MA (licensed moneylender’s failure to hand over the duly stamped moneylending agreement to the borrower before the loan was disbursed to the borrower) but the loan had already been disbursed by the licensed moneylender to the borrower, whether the licensed moneylender could claim for the borrower to return only the outstanding principal sum of the loan (Outstanding Principal Sum) pursuant to - (a) s 66 of the Contracts Act 1950 (CA); or (b) the equitable doctrine of unjust enrichment as laid down by the Federal Court’s judgment in Dream Property Sdn Bhd v Atlas Housing Sdn Bhd [2015] 2 MLJ 441; and (2) if the licensed moneylender is entitled to a return of the Outstanding Principal Sum from the borrower - (a) should the licensed moneylender discharge the charge registered under the Sarawak Land Code (LC) over land which has been used as a security for the repayment of the loan?; and (b) is the licensed moneylender entitled to - (i) interest on the Outstanding Principal Sum from the date of the court’s judgment pursuant to O 42 r 12 of the Rules of Court 2012 (RC); and (ii) claim costs for filing court proceedings to recover the Outstanding Principal Sum from the borrower?
